lessons.title: Standings points and the loser point

payload.prompt: How many points does a team get for a regulation win?

options.text: One point
Two points
options.explanation: Correct. A regulation win is worth two points in the NHL standings.

options.text: Three points

explanation.correct: Right. Two points for a win, one point for an overtime loss, zero for a regulation loss.
explanation.incorrect: In the NHL, a regulation win is worth two points. Overtime losses earn one loser point.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two points for a win, one for losing in overtime.

payload.prompt: A team is 30 wins, 10 losses, 5 overtime losses. How many points?

explanation.correct: Nice. Thirty wins at two points is 60, the five overtime losses add one each for 65, and the ten regulation losses add nothing.
explanation.incorrect: Wins are worth two points and overtime losses one, so 30 x 2 + 5 = 65. The ten regulation losses count as zero.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wins times two, plus the overtime losses.

payload.prompt: Describe the loser point in the NHL standings.
payload.template: A team that loses in {{when}} still gets {{count}} in the standings.

explanation.correct: Exactly. That's the loser point: one point for losing in overtime or a shootout, none for losing in regulation. Fans argue about whether it's fair, and the PWHL has its own version in its 3-2-1-0 system.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL gives one point for an overtime or shootout loss and none for a regulation loss. Playoff games don't have standings points, so the loser point is a regular-season idea.

payload.prompt: Teams tied on points (same games played) are split first by regulation wins. True or false?

scene.alt: Two teams with identical records competing for a playoff position.

explanation.correct: True. With equal points and games played, the NHL looks at regulation wins (RW) first, which rewards teams that win without needing overtime.
explanation.incorrect: When points are tied, the NHL's first tiebreaker is regulation wins, so a win in 60 minutes counts for more than one in overtime or a shootout.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tied on points? Check regulation wins first.

payload.prompt: Overtime in the regular season is 20 minutes of 3-on-3 play. True or false?

scene.alt: Three players per side competing in sudden-death overtime.

explanation.correct: False. Regular-season overtime is five minutes of 3-on-3, not twenty. It is sudden death.
explanation.incorrect: Regulation is three 20-minute periods. Overtime is five minutes, sudden death. First goal wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five minutes of 3-on-3 is all you get in the regular season.

payload.prompt: Describe why 3-on-3 creates scoring chances.
payload.template: With fewer players, there is {{space}} and {{time}} for each skater. The result is {{play}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Fewer skaters mean more space, and more space creates odd-man rushes and one-on-one chances.
explanation.incorrect: With only three skaters a side, there is a lot of open ice for each player. That creates odd-man rushes and breakaway-style chances.

payload.prompt: If neither team scores in overtime, what happens next?

options.text: Another overtime period
A shootout decides the game
options.explanation: Correct. If no goal in five minutes of 3-on-3, it goes to a best-of-three shootout.

options.text: The game is a tie

explanation.correct: Right. Five minutes of 3-on-3, then a shootout. No ties in the regular season.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season uses a shootout after five minutes of overtime. Playoffs go to multiple overtime periods.

payload.prompt: Match the advantage type to what it means in overtime.

pairs.definition: A fast skater thrives in 3-on-3 because there is so much open ice to use.
A skillful skater or passer has more chances to make a play with fewer defenders.
After 60 minutes of hockey, tired legs are a problem in an overtime with so much skating.

explanation.summary: Three-on-three rewards speed and skill, and tired legs hurt. It feels like a different game from five-on-five.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three-on-three is all about speed and space.

lessons.title: The shootout
lessons.objective: Explain how it works and where it does not.

payload.prompt: Order how a shootout happens in the regular season.

items.text: Overtime ends scoreless and each coach picks his shooters.
items.why: A shootout only happens when the five minutes of overtime end tied.

items.text: Teams alternate shooters, each going one-on-one against the goalie.
items.why: Each attempt is a solo chance, like a penalty shot.

items.text: Each team takes three shots, unless one team is out of reach sooner.
items.why: After three shots each, the team with more goals wins the game.

items.text: If it is still tied, sudden death: one shot each until one team scores and the other misses.
items.why: The first team to outscore the other in a round wins.

explanation.correct: That's the order. Shooters alternate, three each, and if it's still tied it goes to sudden death one round at a time.
explanation.incorrect: It runs like this: overtime ends tied, shooters alternate one-on-one, each team gets three shots, and sudden death decides anything still level.

payload.prompt: Does the Stanley Cup Playoffs use a shootout to decide games?

options.text: Yes, after five minutes of overtime
No, playoff games continue in multiple overtime periods until someone scores
options.explanation: Correct. The playoffs have no shootout; they keep playing 20-minute sudden-death periods.

options.text: Yes, but with five shooters per team

explanation.correct: Right. Playoffs are all-or-nothing: no shootout, just overtime until a goal is scored.
explanation.incorrect: The shootout is a regular-season tiebreaker only. Playoffs go to multiple overtime periods until there is a winner.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We lost the shootout even though we had more shots on goal all game.

payload.question: What is the fan describing?

options.text: A shootout is a separate skills contest from five-on-five play
options.explanation: Correct. The shootout is solo shots against the goalie, so it can undo a game they controlled.

options.text: The other team's goalie was better overall
options.explanation: The fan says her team had more shots, so this isn't about goalie quality. It's about the format.

options.text: The referees favored the other team
options.explanation: A shootout is decided by shooters and goalies, not officiating.

payload.translation: A shootout is solo shots against the goalie, so it doesn't reflect who controlled the game. You can dominate five-on-five and still lose it one-on-one.

followUps.line: Did you at least get the extra standings point?
followUps.why: Shows you know a shootout loss still earns the loser point.

followUps.line: Do you like the shootout, or would you rather play more overtime?
followUps.why: Invites her opinion; fans genuinely disagree about it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Shootouts split fans. Asking what she thinks is better than pretending to have a hot take.

payload.prompt: A shootout goal counts toward a player's season goal total. True or false?

scene.alt: A skater scores on a shootout attempt while the goalie lunges.

explanation.correct: False. Shootout goals and saves are tracked separately. The winning team gets one extra goal on the scoreboard, but the shooter's personal goal count doesn't change.
explanation.incorrect: Shootout goals don't go into a player's season total. They're tracked in shootout stats, and the game simply counts as a one-goal win for the victors.

lessons.title: Wild cards and the playoff line

payload.prompt: Match the playoff position to what it means.

pairs.definition: The team with the most points in its division; it gets a playoff spot and a top seed.
One of the two best teams left in a conference after the top three per division; it plays a division winner.
A team outside the top three in its division that also misses both wild cards.

explanation.summary: Sixteen teams make the NHL playoffs: the top three in each of the four divisions, plus two wild cards in each conference.
explanation.sayThisLine: Top three in your division or grab a wild card spot.

payload.prompt: Two games left, one point out of the last wild card. What's the plan?

situation.narrative: Your team trails the final wild card spot by a point with two games to play. The team holding the spot has three left.

facts.label: Position
facts.value: One point out of the last wild card

facts.label: Injury status
facts.value: Top defenseman is day-to-day, not cleared yet

facts.label: Tiebreaker
facts.value: Regulation wins matter if you finish level

options.label: Go for wins, and play the defenseman only if the medical staff clears him
options.consequence: You give yourself the best shot at the playoffs without risking a player's health. Winning in regulation helps if the race ends in a tie.
considerations: Two wins may be enough, so each game matters.
A regulation win is worth the same two points but counts more if you finish level.
A player returns only when the medical staff says he's ready.

options.label: Rest the stars now and save them for next season
options.consequence: You give up a real chance to get in. Fans and teammates notice when a team stops competing with a spot still possible.
considerations: The race is still open, so giving up early is hard to defend.
Resting makes sense only once a team is eliminated.

options.label: Play the defenseman even though he isn't cleared
options.consequence: You might gain a bit of skill on the ice but risk a worse injury that could cost him a playoff run and more.
considerations: Health comes first; teams follow the medical staff's clearance.
A rushed return can hurt him and the team for longer.

payload.expertNote: When a playoff spot is still possible, teams play to win with whoever is healthy, and the medical staff decides who is ready. Resting stars is for teams that are already in or already out.
payload.sayThisLine: They're still in it, so they have to win in regulation.

payload.prompt: Describe how the NHL playoff bracket is built.
payload.template: The {{champ}} in each division make the playoffs, plus {{wc}} wild cards per conference, for {{total}} teams total.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Four divisions with three teams each is twelve, and two wild cards in each conference add four, for sixteen.
explanation.incorrect: The top three teams in each of four divisions make twelve, and each conference adds two wild cards, so sixteen teams in all.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We are a wild card team, and wild cards face the division winner in round one. That is the matchup.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: The team made the playoffs but did not win the division
options.explanation: Correct. Wild cards are playoff teams that did not finish top three in their division.

options.text: The team got a bye in round one
options.explanation: There are no byes in the NHL playoffs. A wild card plays a division winner in round one.

options.text: The team will play another wild card team first
options.explanation: Each wild card is paired with a division winner in round one, not with the other wild card.

payload.translation: The team made the playoffs as a wild card, finishing outside the top three in its division, so in round one it faces a division winner from its own conference.

followUps.line: Who did you draw in round one?
followUps.why: It invites her to share the matchup, which is the fun part.

followUps.line: Did you clinch the wild card on the last night?
followUps.why: A light question that shows you understand how close the playoff line can be.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Wild card seeding confuses plenty of fans. Asking who plays whom beats guessing.

payload.prompt: Order the playoff rounds from first to last.

items.text: Round one: wild cards play division winners; 8 teams advance.
items.why: The first round of the playoffs starts with sixteen teams competing in eight series.

items.text: Round two: the eight winners play four series; four advance.
items.why: After round one, the eight winners pair off again, within their division.

items.text: Round three: conference finals; four teams play two series; two advance.
items.why: The conference finals leave one team per conference.

items.text: Finals: Stanley Cup Final; two teams compete for the Cup.
items.why: The last round is a best-of-seven for the Stanley Cup.

explanation.correct: That's it. Four rounds, each a best-of-seven: 16, then 8, then 4, then 2, then one champion.
explanation.incorrect: There are four rounds, each a best-of-seven. The field goes 16, 8, 4, 2 and finally one champion.

payload.prompt: In a best-of-seven series, how many games must you win to advance?

options.text: Three games
Four games
options.explanation: Correct. The first team to four wins ends the series and advances.

options.text: Five games

explanation.correct: Right. Best-of-seven: first to four wins advances. The series can end in four, five, six, or seven games.
explanation.incorrect: A best-of-seven ends when one team wins four games. You cannot play more than seven games, but you can end early.

payload.prompt: Your team is down 3-1 in a series. How do you approach Game 5?

situation.narrative: Your team trails the series 3 games to 1. Game 5 is at home tonight, and one more loss ends the season.

facts.label: Comebacks from 3-1
facts.value: Rare, but it has happened many times

facts.label: Next step
facts.value: Win Game 5, then Game 6, then Game 7

options.label: Throw caution away and attack all night
options.consequence: You might steal a goal, but a wide-open game invites counterattacks, and one mistake can end the series.
considerations: Desperation can work in one game but leaves you exposed.
An overcommitted team gives up odd-man rushes.

options.label: Play your system and focus on winning just this game
options.consequence: Staying composed keeps you in the game. A win shifts belief, and then you can think about Game 6.
considerations: A series comeback is built one game at a time.
Discipline and solid defense keep you in games you could lose.
You can't win four games at once.

options.label: Write off the series and save energy
options.consequence: Giving in hurts the team and fans. Even down 3-1, you play to win every game and make the other team earn it.
considerations: A team that quits has no chance of a comeback at all.

payload.expertNote: Teams trailing 3-1 don't think about the whole series. They take the next game, then the next one. Fans say 'one game at a time' because that's how comebacks actually happen.
payload.sayThisLine: They're down 3-1, but they only need to win tonight.

payload.prompt: Home ice advantage in the playoffs means your team plays more games at home. True or false?

scene.alt: A rink packed with home fans cheering during a playoff game.

explanation.correct: True. The higher seed hosts four of the seven games (Games 1, 2, 5 and 7), so it gets more time in its own rink and the last change in a Game 7.
explanation.incorrect: Home ice means hosting more games. In a best-of-seven the higher seed plays Games 1, 2, 5 and 7 at home, four of the seven.
explanation.sayThisLine: They have home ice, so Game 7 would be in their building.

lessons.title: The Stanley Cup
lessons.objective: Talk about the Cup and its traditions.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The Stanley Cup is the most storied trophy in hockey. Every winner's name goes on it.

payload.question: What tradition is she describing?

options.text: Engraving: the winning team's names are added to the Cup permanently
options.explanation: Correct. The Stanley Cup is engraved with the names of each champion, year after year.

options.text: Each team gets a copy of the Cup to take home
options.explanation: There is one Cup that gets passed along each year; winners don't each take a copy home. Each one gets to spend a day with it.

options.text: Winners sell their name rights to the Cup
options.explanation: The Cup is not sold or licensed. Engraving a name is a historic honor.

payload.translation: The Stanley Cup is engraved with the names of the players, coaches and staff who win it. That permanence is part of what makes it iconic.

followUps.line: Do players still get a day with the Cup in the summer?
followUps.why: Shows you know about one of the best traditions around it.

followUps.line: Have you ever seen the Cup in person?
followUps.why: A friendly question that lets her tell a story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't know the Cup's traditions yet, asking about them beats guessing a story.

payload.prompt: What trophy does the regular-season points leader get?

options.text: The Stanley Cup
The Presidents' Trophy
options.explanation: Correct. The Presidents' Trophy goes to the team with the best regular-season record, not the playoff champion.

options.text: The Hart Trophy

explanation.correct: Right. The Presidents' Trophy is for the best regular season. The Stanley Cup is for the playoff champion, which is different.
explanation.incorrect: The Presidents' Trophy rewards regular-season success. The Stanley Cup goes to the playoff winner. The best regular season does not guarantee the Cup.

payload.prompt: Order how a team wins the Stanley Cup.

items.text: Finish in the top three of your division or grab a wild card spot.
items.why: You need to make the playoffs first. Regular season puts you in position.

items.text: Win round one (wild cards face division winners).
items.why: Four wins in a best-of-seven series advances you to the next round.

items.text: Win round two against another team from your conference.
items.why: The second round narrows the field to four teams, still within each conference.

items.text: Win the conference final to reach the Stanley Cup Final.
items.why: The conference finals leave one team from each conference.

items.text: Win the Stanley Cup Final in a best-of-seven to claim the championship.
items.why: Four wins in the Cup Final means you are champions and your name goes on the trophy.

explanation.correct: That's the path. Make the playoffs, then win four best-of-seven series and the Cup is yours.
explanation.incorrect: The path to the Cup is: make the playoffs, then win four best-of-seven rounds. Only the conference finals and the Final cross conferences at the end.

payload.prompt: Match the Cup tradition to what it means.

pairs.definition: The names of the winning team's players, coaches and staff are added to the trophy for good.
Each member of the winning team spends a day with the Cup over the summer to celebrate with family and friends.
The presentation of the Cup to the winning team on the ice, often with tears, hugs and celebration.

explanation.summary: The Stanley Cup has traditions, from engraved names to a day with the Cup, that make winning it feel bigger than a trophy. Fans love the stories behind it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Cup traditions are half the reason people love this sport.
